description: Components, props, state — how modern front-ends are built.

screens.body: A front-end framework (like React) lets you build UIs from components instead of hand-writing HTML for every screen. You describe WHAT the UI should look like for a given state — the framework handles updating the page when things change.

options: Describe UI for a given state; the framework updates the page
check.question: A front-end framework lets you…

screens.heading: What a front-end framework does
screens.keyPoint: Describe the UI. Let the framework update it.

screens.body: A component is a reusable piece of UI: a button, a task card, a navbar. You build small components, then compose them into screens. Your SwiftGigs app is components all the way down — TaskCard, ChatBubble, ProfileHeader.
screens.heading: Components

screens.body: State is data that changes over time: the text in an input, whether a menu is open, the list of tasks. In React you store it with useState. When state changes, the framework re-renders the component — you never touch the DOM yourself.

options: Data that changes; UI re-renders when it does
check.question: State is…

code.snippet:
const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
// setCount(1) → UI updates itself

screens.heading: State

screens.body: Props are inputs passed from a parent component to a child — like function arguments. State is internal to the component. Rule of thumb: if a child needs it, pass it as props; if only this component cares, keep it in state.

options: Props come from the parent; state is internal
check.question: Props vs state:

code.snippet:
<TaskCard title="Mow lawn" price={25} />
// title and price are props

screens.heading: Props vs state
screens.keyPoint: Props in from parent. State lives inside.

screens.body: Responsive design means your layout adapts: phone, tablet, desktop. Mobile-first means you design for the small screen first, then expand. Your Learn SD app is mobile-first — that's why it feels like an app on your phone.

options: Layouts that adapt to screen size
Websites that only work on phones
check.question: Responsive design means…

screens.heading: Responsive design

screens.body: In vanilla JS, every UI change means finding elements and updating them by hand — it gets messy fast. Frameworks remove that whole category of bugs: you update state, the UI follows. That's the productivity win your course talks about.
screens.heading: Why frameworks beat vanilla

screens.body: Your Learn SD app is React. The path screen is a component. Each lesson screen is a component. Byte's chat window is a component. When you fix a bug in TaskCard, every task card everywhere is fixed — that's the power.
screens.heading: Your apps are components

screens.body: React docs: react.dev. web.dev: responsive design.
screens.heading: Go deeper
screens.keyPoint: The React docs are genuinely good.
